what: Sibanye Stillwater mines precious metals. It is one of the world’s largest producers of platinum, palladium and rhodium, mined in South Africa and the United States, and also mines gold in South Africa. It has been expanding into battery metals including lithium and nickel.
customers: Metal refiners and traders, and ultimately carmakers, since platinum group metals are used mainly in catalytic converters that clean vehicle exhaust.
money: Platinum, palladium and rhodium from South African and American operations.
Deep-level gold mines in South Africa.
Lithium and nickel projects in Europe and recycling operations.
moat: Platinum group metal deposits are geologically rare and concentrated almost entirely in South Africa and Russia, which makes an operating mine there a genuinely scarce asset. Sibanye also runs a recycling business that recovers metal from spent catalytic converters, which supplies metal without mining it.
risks: South African deep mining is among the most difficult in the world: electricity shortages, labour disputes, safety incidents and shaft depth all raise costs and interrupt production.
Last year’s results showed a 4.0% net loss margin, and revenue fell from $10.8B in 2021 to $5.9B in 2024 before recovering, which shows how violently the earnings swing.
Palladium and rhodium demand comes mainly from petrol vehicle catalytic converters, and electric vehicles need neither — a structural decline that is already underway.
Debt of $2.2B against $849.9M of cash is heavy for a business with earnings this volatile.
Only five analysts cover the stock, so the $12.61 average target rests on thin coverage.
opportunities: Trailing net income of $934.7M on $9.5B of revenue, free cash flow of $507.0M, and the shares at about 6.5 times earnings and 1.8 times EV/EBITDA.
Revenue recovered from $5.9B in 2024 to $7.5B in 2025 as metal prices rose, with trailing revenue of $9.5B.
Platinum group metal deposits are geographically concentrated, so supply cannot expand quickly in response to price.
Platinum has industrial and hydrogen-related uses that do not depend on combustion engines, unlike palladium.
Operating leverage is extreme: at a largely fixed cost base, metal price increases go almost entirely to profit.
watch: All-in sustaining cost per ounce at each operation, and production volumes. South African mining costs rise relentlessly, and the cost per ounce decides whether a strong metal price becomes profit.
view: Sibanye is a leveraged bet on platinum group metal prices operated under some of the hardest mining conditions on earth, and both halves of that sentence matter. The deposits are geologically rare — concentrated almost entirely in South Africa and Russia — which means supply cannot respond quickly to price and the metal is genuinely scarce. The mines are also deep, electricity-constrained, labour-intensive and subject to safety stoppages, which means costs rise every year whatever management does.

The operating leverage this produces is extreme in both directions. Revenue fell from $10.8 billion in 2021 to $5.9 billion in 2024 and the company posted a loss; it has since recovered to $9.5 billion trailing with $935 million of net income. Nothing about the mines changed. Metal prices moved, and because the cost base is largely fixed, almost all of it flowed to the bottom line. At 6.5 times earnings and 1.8 times EV/EBITDA the shares look very cheap, and they would look very expensive again at the previous year’s earnings.

The structural problem deserves more weight than the cheap multiple. Palladium and rhodium are used almost entirely in catalytic converters for petrol engines. Electric vehicles need neither. That is not a cyclical headwind; it is the gradual disappearance of the main source of demand for two of the three metals. Platinum is better placed, with industrial and potential hydrogen uses that do not depend on combustion, but it is also the lowest-priced of the three.

So this is a cheap, highly leveraged producer of a scarce metal whose largest end market is shrinking, operating in a jurisdiction that makes costs rise faster than inflation, with $2.2 billion of debt. It can produce enormous returns in a strong price environment and it can lose money quickly. I would treat it as a trading position in metal prices rather than an investment in a business, and I would judge it on all-in sustaining cost per ounce, which is the only variable management controls and the one that determines whether a high price survives the journey to the income statement.
bull: Platinum group metal prices stay strong against geologically constrained supply, extreme operating leverage converts it to profit, and 1.8 times EV/EBITDA rerates sharply.
bear: Electric vehicles keep eroding palladium and rhodium demand while South African costs rise relentlessly, and $2.2 billion of debt meets another loss-making year.
